posts.title: Why Did Humans Even Invent Computers?

slides.heading: Four hours re-doing a payroll sheet by hand, and I still shipped two wrong cells
slides.bodyText: One broken formula meant redoing thousands of tiny sums manually — and human arithmetic doesn't stay correct at volume.

slides.heading: The bottleneck was never the math. It was us.
slides.bodyText: Each operation was trivial. Doing thousands of them exactly, without fatigue or a slipped digit, is precisely where humans fail.

slides.heading: So we built a machine to do the exact, boring part
slides.bodyText: A computer follows fixed rules over huge amounts of data and returns the same answer every single time — no tiredness, no drift.

slides.heading: Humans bring judgment. Machines bring tireless precision.
slides.bodyText: We kept deciding what to compute; the machine took over doing it — fast, identical, at any scale. That division of labour is the whole point.

slides.heading: Computers exist because humans are slow and error-prone at exact, repetitive work — and machines aren't
slides.bodyText: That one trade-off is the seed of every track that follows.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: The Minds Before Computers Existed

slides.heading: People designed a general-purpose computer a full century before one could be built
slides.bodyText: Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for a machine that didn't physically exist yet.

slides.heading: The hard part was never the wires — it was the idea
slides.bodyText: Before hardware, someone had to imagine a single machine that could follow any set of instructions, not just one fixed task.

slides.heading: Babbage designed it, Lovelace programmed it, Turing proved it
slides.bodyText: Babbage's Analytical Engine had a processor and memory on paper; Lovelace saw it could manipulate symbols, not just numbers; Turing defined what such a machine could and couldn't compute.

slides.heading: A special-purpose machine does one job; a general-purpose one does any job you can describe
slides.bodyText: The leap was from 'a device that adds' to 'a device that runs whatever instructions you feed it.'

slides.heading: The computer was invented as an idea long before it was invented as a machine
slides.bodyText: Hardware caught up to a concept that was already complete.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: From Mainframes to AI Computers: The Full Evolution

posts.title: From Mainframes to AI Computers: The Full Evolution

slides.heading: The same computing idea has fit in a room, a desk, a pocket, and now a data-centre rack
slides.bodyText: Nothing about the core idea changed — only its cost and size.

slides.heading: Each era solved 'who can afford a computer?' one step further
slides.bodyText: Mainframes served whole companies, PCs served individuals, the cloud rents computing by the second, and AI chips specialise it.

slides.heading: Mainframe to PC to cloud to AI accelerator
slides.bodyText: Shrinking transistors made machines cheaper and smaller; the network let us rent them remotely; AI workloads pushed us back toward specialised hardware built for one kind of math.

slides.heading: General-purpose CPUs do anything adequately; AI accelerators do one thing spectacularly
slides.bodyText: We spent decades generalising the computer, then started specialising it again for machine learning.

slides.heading: The computer never got a new idea — it just got cheaper, smaller, and rentable
slides.bodyText: Every revolution in this story is the same machine, more accessible.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: What Is a Computer, Really?

slides.heading: Strip away the screen, the OS, the apps — what's actually left?
slides.bodyText: Underneath everything, a computer is doing four things in a loop.

slides.heading: A computer is a machine that follows instructions over data
slides.bodyText: It takes input, processes it by rule, stores intermediate results, and produces output. That's the entire job description.

slides.heading: Input, process, store, output — on repeat, billions of times a second
slides.bodyText: Data comes in, the processor transforms it step by step using stored instructions, and results go out. Everything else is a layer on top of this cycle.

slides.heading: Instructions and data are both just numbers in memory — the CPU tells them apart by role
slides.bodyText: A byte isn't 'code' or 'data' by nature; it's whichever the processor treats it as right now.

slides.heading: A computer is an instruction-follower, not a thinker — it does exactly what it's told, very fast
slides.bodyText: Its power is obedience at scale, not intelligence.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Von Neumann vs Harvard: Two Ways to Build a Computer

posts.title: Von Neumann vs Harvard: Two Ways to Build a Computer

slides.heading: Two computers can be built on opposite wiring choices and you'd never know from the outside
slides.bodyText: The difference is where instructions and data live.

slides.heading: The question: should code and data share one memory, or get separate ones?
slides.bodyText: Every processor answers this, and the answer shapes speed, flexibility, and safety.

slides.heading: Von Neumann shares one memory bus; Harvard splits instructions and data apart
slides.bodyText: One shared path is simpler and lets programs modify themselves; two separate paths let the CPU fetch an instruction and its data at the same time.

slides.heading: Shared memory: flexible but bottlenecked. Split memory: fast but rigid.
slides.bodyText: Von Neumann's single bus is a traffic jam under load; Harvard's dual bus is faster but harder to reprogram — which is why microcontrollers often use it and general computers don't.

slides.heading: Von Neumann trades speed for flexibility; Harvard trades flexibility for speed
slides.bodyText: The wiring choice is a bet on what the machine will be used for.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: x86 vs ARM: Instruction Set Architectures & Pipelining

posts.title: x86 vs ARM: Instruction Set Architectures & Pipelining

slides.heading: The same app runs on your laptop and your phone, but the chips speak different languages
slides.bodyText: x86 and ARM don't share an instruction set.

slides.heading: An instruction set is the vocabulary a CPU understands
slides.bodyText: x86 offers many complex instructions (CISC); ARM offers fewer, simpler ones (RISC) that the chip runs faster and with less power.

slides.heading: Pipelining lets a CPU work on several instructions at once
slides.bodyText: Like an assembly line, one instruction is decoded while the next is fetched and the previous one executes — simpler instructions keep that line flowing smoothly.

slides.heading: x86: raw performance, more power draw. ARM: efficiency, longer battery.
slides.bodyText: Complex instructions do more per step but stall the pipeline; simple instructions do less per step but keep it full — which is why phones favour ARM and desktops long favoured x86.

slides.heading: CISC packs power into each instruction; RISC packs speed into simple ones done relentlessly
slides.bodyText: Neither is 'better' — they optimise for different constraints.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Bits, Bytes & Binary: The Language of Machines

posts.title: Bits, Bytes & Binary: The Language of Machines

slides.heading: Every photo, song, and message on your machine is really just two symbols: on and off
slides.bodyText: There is nothing else underneath.

slides.heading: A bit is one on/off switch; a byte is eight of them
slides.bodyText: Eight bits give 256 combinations — enough to encode a letter, a small number, or a shade of colour.

slides.heading: Meaning comes from agreed encodings, not from the bits themselves
slides.bodyText: 01000001 is the letter 'A' only because ASCII says so. Change the encoding and the same bits become a number or a pixel.

slides.heading: Binary is fragile in meaning but rock-solid in hardware
slides.bodyText: Two clean voltage levels are trivial for a circuit to tell apart, which is why everything is built on base-2 instead of base-10.

slides.heading: Computers don't store letters or colours — they store switches, and we agree what the switches mean
slides.bodyText: All data is interpretation layered on on/off.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Logic Gates: How Computers Think

slides.heading: How does a box of switches ever 'decide' anything?
slides.bodyText: With three tiny operations, and nothing more.

slides.heading: Logic gates turn on/off inputs into on/off outputs by rule
slides.bodyText: AND outputs on only if both inputs are on; OR if either is; NOT flips its input. That's the entire toolkit.

slides.heading: Combine gates and you can build addition, comparison, memory
slides.bodyText: Wire enough AND/OR/NOT together and you get an adder; loop them back and you get a circuit that remembers a bit.

slides.heading: A single gate is trivial; millions of them wired together is a processor
slides.bodyText: Complexity here isn't clever parts — it's simple parts repeated at enormous scale.

slides.heading: Every 'decision' a computer makes reduces to AND, OR, and NOT on switches
slides.bodyText: Intelligence is not in the gate — it's in the arrangement.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Transistors to CPU: The Brain of the Machine

posts.title: Transistors to CPU: The Brain of the Machine

slides.heading: A modern CPU has billions of transistors, and each one only does one thing
slides.bodyText: A transistor is a switch that electricity controls — no moving parts, just on or off.

slides.heading: A transistor is an electrically-controlled on/off switch
slides.bodyText: Feed it a signal and it opens or closes a circuit. Group a few and you've built a logic gate.

slides.heading: Transistors to gates to ALU to CPU
slides.bodyText: Gates form arithmetic units; arithmetic units plus registers and a control unit form a processor that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions.

slides.heading: Smaller transistors mean more of them, but heat becomes the wall
slides.bodyText: Shrinking lets us pack more computing into a chip — until the density traps so much heat that speed gains stall. That's why clock speeds plateaued.

slides.heading: A CPU is billions of the same tiny switch, arranged to fetch, decode, and execute
slides.bodyText: The brain of the machine is repetition, not magic.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Cache, RAM & Storage: Where Computers Keep Memories

posts.title: Cache, RAM & Storage: Where Computers Keep Memories

slides.heading: Why does your machine have RAM and storage instead of just one big memory?
slides.bodyText: Because no single memory is both fast and cheap.

slides.heading: Memory forms a hierarchy: cache, RAM, disk
slides.bodyText: Cache is tiny and blazing fast, RAM is larger and fast, storage is huge and slow but keeps data when the power is off.

slides.heading: The CPU checks the fastest memory first, falling back as it misses
slides.bodyText: Wanted data in cache? Instant. Not there? Check RAM. Not there? Load from disk — orders of magnitude slower each step down.

slides.heading: Speed, capacity, and cost pull against each other
slides.bodyText: Fast memory is expensive and small; cheap memory is slow and large. The hierarchy is how we get the feel of fast-and-huge without paying for it.

slides.heading: The memory hierarchy is a bet: keep what you'll need soon close, and everything else far but cheap
slides.bodyText: Fast, big, cheap — pick two, then layer them.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: GPU, Motherboard & I/O: Completing the Machine

posts.title: GPU, Motherboard & I/O: Completing the Machine

slides.heading: The CPU gets all the credit, but it can't draw a pixel or save a file alone
slides.bodyText: It needs the rest of the machine.

slides.heading: GPU, motherboard, and I/O complete the computer
slides.bodyText: The GPU does massively parallel work like graphics; the motherboard's buses connect everything; I/O moves data between the machine and the outside world.

slides.heading: A CPU does a few things fast in sequence; a GPU does thousands of things at once
slides.bodyText: For one hard calculation, the CPU wins. For the same simple calculation on a million pixels, the GPU's parallel cores win — which is also why they run AI math.

slides.heading: Buses trade simplicity for shared bandwidth
slides.bodyText: One shared pathway keeps the design simple but forces components to take turns; dedicated lanes are faster but cost more wiring and pins.

slides.heading: The CPU thinks in sequence, the GPU thinks in parallel, and buses let them all talk
slides.bodyText: A computer is a team of specialised parts, not one hero chip.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: From Machine Code to Real Programming Languages

posts.title: From Machine Code to Real Programming Languages

slides.heading: Nobody writes real software in ones and zeros — so how did we escape machine code?
slides.bodyText: By stacking layers of translation.

slides.heading: Programming languages are abstractions over machine code
slides.bodyText: Machine code is raw numbers the CPU runs; assembly names those numbers; high-level languages let you write intent that gets translated down to them.

slides.heading: Each layer trades control for readability
slides.bodyText: Assembly maps almost one-to-one to CPU instructions; a language like Python hides registers and memory entirely so you can think in problems, not hardware.

slides.heading: Low-level: total control, painful to write. High-level: fast to write, less control.
slides.bodyText: You give up knowing exactly what the CPU does in exchange for expressing ideas in far less code — usually a good trade, occasionally not.

slides.heading: A programming language is a human-readable disguise over machine code
slides.bodyText: We didn't make the CPU smarter — we made the instructions easier to write.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Compilers vs Interpreters: What Actually Runs Your Code

posts.title: Compilers vs Interpreters: What Actually Runs Your Code

slides.heading: Your source code can't run — the CPU has never seen a for-loop in its life
slides.bodyText: Something has to translate it first.

slides.heading: Compilers and interpreters both bridge source code to machine code — differently
slides.bodyText: A compiler translates the whole program ahead of time into an executable; an interpreter translates and runs it line by line as it goes.

slides.heading: Compile once and run fast, or skip the wait and run as you go
slides.bodyText: Compiled code starts slower to build but runs fast and ships as a standalone binary; interpreted code runs immediately but re-translates every time it executes.

slides.heading: Compilers trade startup time for run speed; interpreters trade run speed for flexibility
slides.bodyText: C compiles to fast native binaries but must be rebuilt; Python runs instantly and portably but pays a speed cost each execution.

slides.heading: Compile now to run fast later, or interpret now to run flexibly today
slides.bodyText: Same goal, opposite timing of the translation.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: What Really Happens Inside Your Computer When You Run a Program

posts.title: What Really Happens Inside Your Computer When You Run a Program

slides.heading: You double-click an app. Between that click and the window opening, a lot happens.
slides.bodyText: Here's the actual sequence.

slides.heading: Running a program means loading its instructions into memory and pointing the CPU at them
slides.bodyText: The file on disk is inert; execution is the OS copying it into RAM and handing control to the CPU.

slides.heading: Source, translate, load, execute
slides.bodyText: Code is compiled or interpreted into machine instructions, the OS loads the program into memory as a process, and the CPU fetches and runs those instructions one by one.

slides.heading: On disk a program is data; in memory it's a running process
slides.bodyText: The same bytes are passive storage until the OS gives them a slice of memory, CPU time, and the right to act.

slides.heading: A program is just a file until the OS loads it into memory and lets the CPU run it
slides.bodyText: Execution is a file being given life by the operating system.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Why Does Every Computer Need an Operating System?

slides.heading: Your laptop runs a browser, music, and twenty background tasks — none of them fighting over the CPU
slides.bodyText: Something is refereeing all of it. That something is the Operating System.

slides.heading: An operating system manages hardware and provides services for programs
slides.bodyText: It allocates CPU time, memory, and I/O devices. It acts as an intermediary between user applications and the bare metal, providing abstractions like files, processes, and a user interface.

slides.heading: The OS boots, loads the kernel, then launches system services and user programs
slides.bodyText: On startup, the bootloader loads the kernel into memory. The kernel initialises hardware, mounts filesystems, and starts system services (daemons). Finally, it presents a login prompt or GUI for user interaction.

slides.heading: Without an OS, one program owns everything; with one, everything shares safely
slides.bodyText: Direct hardware access is fast but chaotic. A managed layer costs a little overhead to buy multitasking, isolation, and security — the OS is the referee that makes it work.

slides.heading: The OS is the referee that lets many programs share one machine without stepping on each other
slides.bodyText: Its job is arbitration, resource management, and providing a stable environment for applications.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Processes & Execution

slides.heading: A program on disk is just a file — but when it runs, it becomes a living entity
slides.bodyText: That living entity is called a process.

slides.heading: A process is a program in execution, with its own address space and resources
slides.bodyText: The Process Control Block (PCB) stores its state (program counter, registers, memory limits). The OS manages process lifecycle: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.

slides.heading: Create → Ready → Running → Waiting/Terminated
slides.bodyText: A process is created by fork() or spawn(). The scheduler picks a ready process to run. It may wait for I/O (blocked) or finish. ConbodyText switching saves/restores the PCB to switch between processes.

slides.heading: Processes are isolated; threads share memory within a process
slides.bodyText: Each process has its own memory space, so one crash doesn't affect others. Threads are lighter — they share memory, making communication fast but also riskier.

slides.heading: The OS gives every program the illusion of having its own CPU and memory
slides.bodyText: Through processes, conbodyText switching, and virtual memory, it turns one machine into many virtual machines.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: CPU Scheduling Policies

slides.heading: With more processes than cores, the OS must decide who runs next — and that choice shapes performance
slides.bodyText: CPU scheduling is the art of managing processor time.

slides.heading: Scheduling policies decide which ready process gets the CPU and for how long
slides.bodyText: Common policies: FCFS (First Come First Served), SJF (Shortest Job First), Round Robin (preemptive time slices), Priority Scheduling, and Multilevel Queue. Metrics: throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, response time.

slides.heading: The scheduler picks a process from the ready queue, dispatches it, and preempts when time expires
slides.bodyText: The dispatcher gives control to the selected process. If the process blocks or its time quantum expires, the scheduler saves its state and picks the next process from the ready queue.

slides.heading: SJF minimises average wait time; Round Robin ensures fairness but has overhead
slides.bodyText: SJF is optimal for turnaround time but requires knowing burst times ahead. Round Robin gives each process a fair slice, good for interactive systems, but conbodyText switching overhead can be high.

slides.heading: No single scheduler is best — pick one that matches your workload's priority (throughput vs latency)
slides.bodyText: Batch systems favour SJF; interactive systems favour Round Robin; real-time systems use priority-based scheduling.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Concurrency & Synchronization

slides.heading: Two processes updating the same variable — without coordination, the result is unpredictable
slides.bodyText: That's a race condition, and synchronization prevents it.

slides.heading: Synchronization ensures orderly access to shared resources using locks, semaphores, or monitors
slides.bodyText: The critical section is a code segment that accesses shared data. Mutual exclusion guarantees only one process enters at a time. Semaphores (counting/binary) and mutexes are common tools.

slides.heading: Enter critical section, acquire lock, access shared data, release lock
slides.bodyText: A process acquires a lock before entering the critical section. After finishing, it releases the lock. If the lock is held, other processes wait — preventing data corruption.

slides.heading: Semaphores are flexible but error‑prone; monitors (like in Java) provide higher‑level structure
slides.bodyText: Semaphores allow arbitrary increments/decrements, making them powerful but easy to misuse. Monitors encapsulate shared data and methods with implicit locking, reducing bugs.

slides.heading: Synchronization is the discipline that makes concurrent programming safe
slides.bodyText: Without it, shared data quickly becomes inconsistent and unreliable.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Deadlock Strategies

slides.heading: Two processes each holding a resource the other needs — and neither will let go — that's a deadlock
slides.bodyText: Deadlocks bring systems to a grinding halt.

slides.heading: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
slides.bodyText: Break any one condition and deadlock is impossible. Prevention eliminates one condition; Avoidance uses algorithms like Banker's to stay in safe states; Detection & Recovery allows deadlock and fixes it.

slides.heading: Detection: build a resource allocation graph; Recovery: terminate a process or preempt resources
slides.bodyText: If the graph has a cycle, deadlock exists. Recovery options: abort one or more processes, or forcibly take resources from a victim (rollback). Often, the simplest recovery is a system restart.

slides.heading: Prevention is safe but conservative; Avoidance is dynamic; Detection & Recovery is pragmatic
slides.bodyText: Prevention may underutilize resources. Avoidance (Banker's) requires knowing future requests. Detection allows maximum resource usage but recovery costs time.

slides.heading: Deadlock is a design flaw, not a bug — the strategy you choose depends on the system's needs
slides.bodyText: Critical systems (banking) use prevention; general‑purpose OSes often use detection and recovery.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Main Memory Architecture

slides.heading: RAM is fast but expensive — and there's never enough. The OS makes it seem like there is
slides.bodyText: Memory management is the art of illusion.

slides.heading: Memory management handles allocation, protection, and sharing of physical memory
slides.bodyText: Logical addresses (virtual) are mapped to physical addresses. Contiguous allocation (fixed partitions) vs non‑contiguous (paging, segmentation). Fragmentation (internal/external) is managed with compaction or paging.

slides.heading: A program uses logical addresses; the MMU translates them to physical addresses
slides.bodyText: The CPU generates logical addresses. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) uses page tables to translate them to physical addresses. Paging breaks memory into fixed‑size frames and pages.

slides.heading: Paging eliminates external fragmentation; segmentation provides logical structuring
slides.bodyText: Paging maps pages to frames — easy to manage but no logical grouping. Segmentation splits memory by logical units (code, data, stack) but can cause external fragmentation.

slides.heading: Memory management gives every program a private address space — and makes RAM feel larger than it is
slides.bodyText: Through paging, segmentation, and virtual memory, the OS creates the illusion of unlimited memory.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Virtual Memory & Paging

slides.heading: You've opened more tabs than you have RAM, and nothing crashed — where did the extra memory come from?
slides.bodyText: Virtual memory makes it possible.

slides.heading: Virtual memory uses disk as an extension of RAM, via demand paging
slides.bodyText: Pages are loaded into RAM only when needed (demand paging). When RAM is full, a page replacement algorithm (LRU, FIFO, Optimal) swaps out less‑used pages. Page tables map virtual to physical frames.

slides.heading: The CPU tries to access a page; if it's not in RAM, a page fault occurs; the OS loads it from disk
slides.bodyText: On a page fault, the OS finds a free frame or evicts a page. It loads the needed page from swap space, updates the page table, and restarts the instruction. This is repeated many times per second.

slides.heading: LRU approximates optimal but has overhead; FIFO is simple but can cause Belady's anomaly
slides.bodyText: Optimal replacement (theoretical) evicts the page used farthest in the future. LRU evicts the least recently used — practical but requires tracking. FIFO is easy but sometimes increases page faults with more frames.

slides.heading: Virtual memory makes programs fit into memory that is physically too small — at the cost of speed
slides.bodyText: It's the reason modern multitasking works at all. Thrashing (constant swapping) is the price of over‑committing.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: File Systems & Storage

slides.heading: Files are the persistent memory of a computer — and they're stored on disks, which are slow
slides.bodyText: File systems and disk scheduling make storage usable.

slides.heading: A file system organises data into files and directories; disk scheduling optimises access
slides.bodyText: File attributes include name, size, permissions. Directories map file names to inodes. Disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, LOOK) reduce seek time by ordering requests.

slides.heading: A file is opened, read/written, and closed; the disk scheduler orders pending I/O requests
slides.bodyText: The OS reads file metadata from the directory, locates data blocks via inodes, and issues disk reads. The scheduler reorders requests to minimise mechanical movement (head seeks).

slides.heading: SSTF minimises average seek time; SCAN provides fairness; FCFS is simple but inefficient
slides.bodyText: SSTF may starve distant requests. SCAN moves across the disk servicing requests in one direction — fairer and predictable. FCFS processes in arrival order, which can cause long waits.

slides.heading: File systems provide structure; disk scheduling provides speed — together they make storage reliable
slides.bodyText: Good file system design and scheduling are critical for overall system performance.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Input/Output Management

slides.heading: The CPU is fast — but disks, keyboards, and networks are painfully slow
slides.bodyText: I/O management bridges this speed gap.

slides.heading: I/O management handles communication between the CPU and peripherals
slides.bodyText: Programmed I/O (polling) — CPU waits for I/O. Interrupt‑driven I/O — CPU does other work until I/O interrupts. DMA (Direct Memory Access) — device moves data directly to/from memory without CPU involvement.

slides.heading: A request is sent, the device processes it, and the OS handles completion (interrupt or polling)
slides.bodyText: The OS issues a command to the device controller. The controller performs the I/O and either interrupts the CPU or sets a status bit. The OS copies data from the controller's buffer to user memory.

slides.heading: Polling wastes CPU cycles; interrupts use CPU only when needed; DMA offloads CPU entirely
slides.bodyText: Polling is simple but burns CPU. Interrupts are efficient for sporadic I/O. DMA is best for large data transfers (disk, network) because it frees the CPU to do other work.

slides.heading: I/O management hides device complexity from applications and minimises CPU idle time
slides.bodyText: Through buffering, caching, and spooling, it makes slow devices feel fast.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Operating System Models

slides.heading: Not all operating systems are the same — some run servers, some run pacemakers, some run toasters
slides.bodyText: OS designs are tailored to their purpose.

slides.heading: OS models vary in architecture: monolithic, microkernel, modular, and hybrid
slides.bodyText: Monolithic (Linux, Unix) — all OS services in one large kernel, fast but less modular. Microkernel (Minix) — minimal kernel, most services in user space, more stable but slower. Modular — combines the two.

slides.heading: Each model balances performance, security, and maintainability differently
slides.bodyText: Monolithic systems make system calls directly into the kernel. Microkernel systems use message passing between user‑space servers, adding overhead but improving fault isolation.

slides.heading: Monolithic is fast but risky; microkernel is safer but slower; modular is a middle path
slides.bodyText: Monolithic: one crash brings down the system. Microkernel: a driver crash can be restarted without rebooting. Modular: loadable kernel modules give flexibility without full monolithic risk.

slides.heading: The OS architecture reflects its design priorities: speed, stability, or both
slides.bodyText: Linux is monolithic; Windows is hybrid; real‑time OSes are often microkernel‑based for predictability.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Real‑World OS Variants

slides.heading: Linux runs the cloud, Windows runs desktops, macOS runs creatives — each with its own philosophy
slides.bodyText: The big three dominate the real world.

slides.heading: Linux: open‑source, server‑dominant. Windows: commercial, desktop‑focused. macOS: Unix‑based, consumer‑oriented
slides.bodyText: Linux is monolithic, highly customisable, and free. Windows has a hybrid kernel with strong backward compatibility. macOS uses a Mach microkernel + BSD, blending Unix power with a polished UI.

slides.heading: Each OS provides a kernel, system libraries, and a user interface — but with different trade‑offs
slides.bodyText: Linux: shell/CLI + GUI (GNOME/KDE). Windows: GUI‑first with PowerShell. macOS: Aqua GUI with Terminal underneath. All support multitasking, memory protection, and networking.

slides.heading: Linux is flexible and low‑cost; Windows has wide software support; macOS integrates well with Apple hardware
slides.bodyText: Linux: thousands of distributions for every need. Windows: unmatched desktop app ecosystem and gaming. macOS: seamless integration with iPhones, iPads, and creative tools.

slides.heading: No OS is 'best' — each solves a different set of problems for different users
slides.bodyText: Choose by ecosystem, cost, hardware, and personal preference. Linux dominates servers; Windows dominates enterprise; macOS dominates creative and consumer spaces.

slides.heading: You've completed the Operating Systems track
slides.bodyText: From boot to processes, scheduling to file systems — you now understand the core of every modern OS.

slides.heading: 'Just tell the computer what to do' — except it does exactly what you say, not what you mean
slides.bodyText: That gap is the whole craft.

slides.heading: Programming is expressing a solution as instructions precise enough for a machine
slides.bodyText: The hard part isn't syntax — it's turning a fuzzy human goal into unambiguous, ordered steps.

slides.heading: You break a problem into steps, encode them, and the machine executes literally
slides.bodyText: No step can be assumed. The computer has no common sense to fill gaps, so every case must be spelled out.

slides.heading: Humans tolerate ambiguity; computers punish it
slides.bodyText: A recipe that says 'season to taste' works for a cook and fails for a machine — programming is removing every 'to taste.'

slides.heading: Programming is the art of being so precise that a machine can't misunderstand you
slides.bodyText: It's specifying, not suggesting.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Imperative vs Declarative: Two Ways to Tell a Computer What to Do

posts.title: Imperative vs Declarative: Two Ways to Tell a Computer What to Do

slides.heading: Two programs solve the same task — one lists every step, the other just describes the result
slides.bodyText: Both are valid. They're opposite styles.

slides.heading: Imperative code says how; declarative code says what
slides.bodyText: Imperative spells out each step to reach the answer; declarative states the goal and lets the system figure out the steps.

slides.heading: A loop that filters a list vs a query that describes the filter
slides.bodyText: Writing 'for each item, if it matches, keep it' is imperative; writing 'give me items where x is true' (like SQL) is declarative.

slides.heading: Imperative gives control; declarative gives brevity
slides.bodyText: Step-by-step code lets you tune exactly how work happens; describing the outcome is shorter and clearer but hides — and limits — your control over the how.

slides.heading: Imperative tells the computer the steps; declarative tells it the destination
slides.bodyText: Choose control or clarity depending on which the problem needs.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: The Building Blocks Every Programmer Learns First

posts.title: The Building Blocks Every Programmer Learns First

slides.heading: Almost every program you'll ever write is built from the same four ideas
slides.bodyText: Master these and the rest is variation.

slides.heading: Variables, conditionals, loops, and functions are the core
slides.bodyText: Variables hold state, conditionals choose paths, loops repeat work, and functions package logic to reuse.

slides.heading: Combine the four and you can express any computation
slides.bodyText: Store a value, branch on it, repeat over a collection, and factor the repeated part into a function — that's the shape of nearly all code.

slides.heading: More abstraction (functions) reduces repetition but adds indirection
slides.bodyText: Pulling logic into functions keeps code DRY and readable; overdo it and a reader has to jump around to follow a simple flow.

slides.heading: Variables, conditionals, loops, functions — every program is a remix of these four
slides.bodyText: Learn the primitives and languages become dialects.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Functional Programming: Pure Functions & Immutability

slides.heading: A function that changes nothing but its return value is weirdly easy to trust
slides.bodyText: That's the whole pitch of functional programming.

slides.heading: Pure functions and immutability are the core of the functional style
slides.bodyText: A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself; immutable data is never modified in place, only copied.

slides.heading: No hidden state means no surprise bugs from shared data
slides.bodyText: Because a pure function can't secretly alter something elsewhere, you can test it in isolation and reason about it without tracking the rest of the program.

slides.heading: Purity buys predictability; it costs some performance and convenience
slides.bodyText: Copying data instead of mutating it is safer and easier to parallelise, but creates more objects and can feel verbose for simple in-place updates.

slides.heading: A pure function is a promise: same input in, same output out, nothing touched on the side
slides.bodyText: Predictability is the feature you're buying.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Scope, Recursion & Handling Errors Like a Pro

posts.title: Scope, Recursion & Handling Errors Like a Pro

slides.heading: A variable that worked everywhere suddenly 'doesn't exist' — welcome to scope
slides.bodyText: Where a name lives decides where it works.

slides.heading: Scope defines where a name is visible; recursion is a function calling itself
slides.bodyText: Variables declared inside a function usually can't be seen outside it; a recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece.

slides.heading: Recursion needs a base case, or it never stops
slides.bodyText: Each call must shrink the problem and there must be a case that returns without recursing — miss it and the call stack overflows.

slides.heading: Recursion is elegant for nested problems but heavier than a loop
slides.bodyText: It reads cleanly for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call uses stack memory a loop wouldn't — deep recursion can crash where a loop wouldn't.

slides.heading: Scope decides where a name lives; recursion works only if it knows when to stop
slides.bodyText: Both are about boundaries — of visibility and of repetition.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Modules, Libraries, Packages & APIs Explained

slides.heading: You'll write far less code than you import — most software is other people's code
slides.bodyText: Reuse is the norm, not the exception.

slides.heading: Modules, libraries, packages, and APIs are all about reusing code
slides.bodyText: A module is a file of related code; a library is a bundle you call; a package is a shippable library; an API is the agreed way to call code you don't own.

slides.heading: You import a package, call its functions through its API, and skip reinventing it
slides.bodyText: Instead of writing date-parsing or HTTP handling yourself, you pull in a tested package and use its documented interface.

slides.heading: Dependencies save time but become risk you don't control
slides.bodyText: Reusing a library is faster and better-tested than DIY, but every dependency adds surface area for bugs, breaking changes, and security holes.

slides.heading: An API is a contract: use this code without knowing how it works inside
slides.bodyText: Reuse is leverage — and a debt you take on.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: What Is an Algorithm? (And Why Coding Is Not Problem Solving)

posts.title: What Is an Algorithm? (And Why Coding Is Not Problem Solving)

slides.heading: You can know every language feature and still not be able to solve the problem
slides.bodyText: Coding and problem-solving are different skills.

slides.heading: An algorithm is a precise, finite procedure that solves a class of problems
slides.bodyText: It's the strategy — the sequence of steps that turns any valid input into the correct output — independent of the language you write it in.

slides.heading: Understand the problem, design the steps, then translate to code
slides.bodyText: The thinking happens before the typing: what are the inputs, the constraints, the approach? Code is just the last step.

slides.heading: Syntax is learnable in weeks; algorithmic thinking takes real practice
slides.bodyText: Knowing how to write a loop is easy; knowing which loop, over what structure, in what order, is the skill that transfers across every language.

slides.heading: Coding is how you tell the computer; the algorithm is what you decided to tell it
slides.bodyText: The problem is solved before a single line is written.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Big O Notation: The Skill That Separates Junior From Senior

posts.title: Big O Notation: The Skill That Separates Junior From Senior

slides.heading: Your code ran fine in the demo and timed out on real data — the difference is Big O
slides.bodyText: It's the skill that separates junior from senior.

slides.heading: Big O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as input grows
slides.bodyText: It ignores seconds and hardware and asks the only question that scales: when the input gets 10x bigger, does the work get 10x, 100x, or barely bigger?

slides.heading: O(1), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) — the shape matters more than the constant
slides.bodyText: A nested loop is O(n²): fine at 100 items, catastrophic at a million. A single pass is O(n). A good sort is O(n log n).

slides.heading: A slower Big O beats a faster machine at scale, every time
slides.bodyText: Throwing hardware at an O(n²) algorithm buys a little room; changing it to O(n log n) buys orders of magnitude — that's why the curve, not the constant, decides.

slides.heading: Big O isn't about how fast it runs — it's about how badly it breaks when the input grows
slides.bodyText: Optimise the growth curve before the constant.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Arrays, Strings & Linked Lists: Where Everyone Starts

posts.title: Arrays, Strings & Linked Lists: Where Everyone Starts

slides.heading: Arrays
slides.bodyText: Think of a movie theater: seat 47 is seat 47, no scanning seats 1-46 to find it. That's an array — a fixed-size, ordered block of memory where every item sits at a numbered position, so reading any item is instant (O(1)), no matter the size.

slides.heading: Strings
slides.bodyText: A string is just an array of characters treated as bodyText — same rules apply: fast to read by position, but its size is locked in from the moment it's created.

slides.heading: Linked Lists
slides.bodyText: Like a treasure hunt where each clue only reveals the next one: a linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next. Inserting is just two pointer updates — instant, even in a list of 10 million. The tradeoff: to find anything, you start at the beginning and follow the chain, one step at a time.

slides.heading: Stack
slides.bodyText: Picture a stack of plates — you only ever add or remove from the top, never the middle or bottom. That's Last-In-First-Out. It's why Ctrl+Z works, why your browser's back button peels off the most recent page first, and how the call stack Collections which function returns next.

slides.heading: Queue
slides.bodyText: A queue is a line at a coffee shop — first person in line, first one served, no cutting. Enqueue adds to the back, dequeue removes from the front. It's how print jobs line up and how web servers process thousands of incoming requests in order.

slides.heading: Hash Tables
slides.bodyText: Search 'mom' in your contacts and her number appears instantly — that's a hash table. A hash function turns the key into a number that points straight to a memory slot, so lookup is O(1) whether you have 10 contacts or 10 million. The cost: more memory, and occasional collisions when two keys land on the same slot.

posts.title: Trees, Heaps & Graphs: Where DSA Gets Real

slides.heading: Trees
slides.bodyText: Open your file explorer: one root at the top, branching into folders, then files — every path flows one direction, root to leaves, with no cycles. That's a tree. HTML's DOM, comment threads, and decision trees all follow the same branching shape.

slides.heading: Heaps
slides.bodyText: Like an ER: the heart attack patient gets seen before the headache, no matter who arrived first. A heap keeps the highest-priority item at the top at all times, reorganizing itself on every insert or removal — which is exactly how OS task schedulers and GPS route recalculation work.

slides.heading: Graphs
slides.bodyText: Facebook is one giant graph — you're a node, friendships are edges. Google Maps is another — cities are nodes, roads are edges, and 'get directions' is just a search across it. Graphs can be directed (Twitter follows) or undirected (Facebook friends), stored as an adjacency matrix (fast lookups) or adjacency list (more memory-efficient), and explored with DFS or BFS.

posts.title: Searching & Sorting: The Algorithms Behind Everything

slides.heading: 'Find this item' and 'put these in order' are behind a shocking amount of software
slides.bodyText: Searching and sorting are everywhere.

slides.heading: Searching finds an item; sorting arranges items so searching gets cheaper
slides.bodyText: Sorted data unlocks fast lookups; much of the value of sorting is making later searches efficient.

slides.heading: Binary search halves the problem each step — but only on sorted data
slides.bodyText: Linear search checks every item; binary search jumps to the middle and discards half each time, turning a million-item search into about twenty steps.

slides.heading: Faster search needs sorted data, and good sorting costs O(n log n)
slides.bodyText: You pay the sort once to make every future search O(log n) — worth it when you search often, wasteful when you search once.

slides.heading: Sort once to search fast forever — the two algorithms pay for each other
slides.bodyText: Order is an investment that searching cashes in.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Recursion, Backtracking, Greedy & DP: The Hard Stuff

posts.title: Recursion, Backtracking, Greedy & DP: The Hard Stuff

slides.heading: Some problems have too many possibilities to brute-force and too much overlap to ignore
slides.bodyText: This is where the hard techniques earn their keep.

slides.heading: Recursion, backtracking, greedy, and dynamic programming are problem-solving strategies
slides.bodyText: Recursion breaks a problem into smaller copies; backtracking tries paths and undoes dead ends; greedy takes the best local step; DP caches overlapping subproblems.

slides.heading: DP turns exponential recursion into something practical by remembering answers
slides.bodyText: A naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values millions of times; storing each result once collapses it from exponential to linear.

slides.heading: Greedy is fast but can be wrong; DP is correct but costs memory
slides.bodyText: A greedy choice is quick and sometimes optimal; dynamic programming guarantees the best answer but stores every subproblem — time for space.

slides.heading: Backtracking explores, greedy gambles, DP remembers — the hard problems need the right strategy, not more speed
slides.bodyText: Technique beats brute force where the search space explodes.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Software Engineering vs Just Writing Code

posts.title: Software Engineering vs Just Writing Code

slides.heading: The code was fine. The project still failed — late, unmaintainable, and impossible to hand off.
slides.bodyText: Writing code and engineering software aren't the same job.

slides.heading: Software engineering is building software that survives people, time, and change
slides.bodyText: It adds the things a working script lacks: tests, version control, documentation, review, and a design that others can extend.

slides.heading: Engineering optimises for the second reader and the sixth month
slides.bodyText: Code is written once and read many times; the discipline is making it correct, understandable, and changeable long after you've forgotten it.

slides.heading: A clever script solves today; engineered software keeps solving as requirements shift
slides.bodyText: Raw coding wins a hackathon; engineering wins the five years of maintenance nobody demos.

slides.heading: Writing code makes it work once; software engineering makes it keep working as everything changes
slides.bodyText: The hard part is not the first version — it's the fiftieth.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: The Software Lifecycle: Build, Test, Ship, Maintain

posts.title: The Software Lifecycle: Build, Test, Ship, Maintain

slides.heading: Shipping isn't the finish line — most of a product's life happens after launch
slides.bodyText: The lifecycle keeps going.

slides.heading: The software lifecycle is build, test, ship, maintain — on repeat
slides.bodyText: Software is planned, built, verified, released, then monitored and changed continuously as bugs and needs surface.

slides.heading: Each stage feeds the next, and maintenance loops back to build
slides.bodyText: Requirements shape the build; tests gate the ship; production feedback becomes the next round of requirements. It's a cycle, not a line.

slides.heading: Rushing to ship trades short-term speed for long-term maintenance cost
slides.bodyText: Skipping tests and design gets you live faster and buys you a slower, riskier every-release after that — the debt compounds.

slides.heading: Software is never 'done' — it's shipped, watched, and changed for as long as anyone uses it
slides.bodyText: Launch is the middle of the story, not the end.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Git, GitHub & How Teams Actually Collaborate on Code

posts.title: Git, GitHub & How Teams Actually Collaborate on Code

slides.heading: Two people edited the same file and one of them lost a day of work — before Git
slides.bodyText: Version control exists so that never happens.

slides.heading: Git Collections every change; GitHub hosts it so teams can collaborate
slides.bodyText: Git records snapshots of your code over time and lets branches diverge and merge; GitHub is the shared home where those histories live and get reviewed.

slides.heading: Branch, commit, push, pull request, merge
slides.bodyText: You work on a branch, save changes as commits, push them up, open a pull request for review, and merge once approved — history stays intact and blame is traceable.

slides.heading: Branching enables parallel work but creates merge conflicts to resolve
slides.bodyText: Everyone working independently is the point; the cost is reconciling changes that touched the same lines — conflicts are the tax on parallelism.

slides.heading: Git is a time machine for code; branches let a team edit the same project without overwriting each other
slides.bodyText: Version control turns collaboration from chaos into history.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Clean Code, SOLID & Design Patterns

slides.heading: The feature worked, but nobody — including you next month — could safely change it
slides.bodyText: Working code isn't the same as good code.

slides.heading: Clean code, SOLID, and design patterns make code changeable, not just correct
slides.bodyText: Clean code is readable and simple; SOLID is five principles for structuring classes; patterns are reusable solutions to recurring design problems.

slides.heading: Good structure isolates change so one edit doesn't ripple everywhere
slides.bodyText: When responsibilities are separated and dependencies point the right way, a new requirement touches one place instead of ten.

slides.heading: Structure costs upfront effort and buys cheaper future change
slides.bodyText: Applying principles and patterns is slower to write and easier to extend; skipping them is faster today and a tangle tomorrow — and patterns overused become their own mess.

slides.heading: Clean code optimises for the human who edits it next — usually a tired version of you
slides.bodyText: Readability is a feature, not a luxury.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Network Topologies & The Devices That Move Data

slides.heading: Every device you own is part of a silent conversation — how do they talk?
slides.bodyText: From your phone to the server halfway across the world, they all share data through a hidden system: a computer network.

slides.heading: A computer network is a group of interconnected devices that share data and resources
slides.bodyText: Devices (nodes) communicate via wired or wireless links, following rules (protocols). Networks enable email, file sharing, web browsing, and remote access.

slides.heading: How does data actually move?
slides.bodyText: Each device gets a unique IP address. Data is broken into packets, labelled with source/destination, routed by switches and routers, and reassembled at the receiving end — all governed by protocols.

slides.heading: Networks bring huge advantages, but also risks
slides.bodyText: Pros: resource sharing, fast communication, centralised storage, remote access. Cons: security threats, setup cost, maintenance, single‑point‑of‑failure risks.

slides.heading: A network is the backbone of modern computing — without it, we'd still be moving files by hand
slides.bodyText: It's a system of nodes, links, and rules that makes global connectivity possible.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Network Topologies & Devices

slides.heading: The shape of a network determines how resilient and fast it is
slides.bodyText: Star, mesh, bus — each topology has its own trade‑offs in cost, performance, and fault tolerance.

slides.heading: Topology is the physical or logical layout of connections
slides.bodyText: Star: all devices connect to a central hub. Mesh: every device connects to every other. Bus: all share a single line. Devices like switches, routers, and hubs forward traffic along these links.

slides.heading: Data travels from source to destination through a series of hops
slides.bodyText: A switch forwards frames within a local network. A router moves packets between different networks. The chosen topology decides how many alternative paths exist and how failures affect the whole.

slides.heading: Star is simple but fragile; mesh is resilient but expensive
slides.bodyText: A star network hinges on one central device — if it fails, the whole network goes down. A mesh has many redundant links, but cabling and configuration costs are much higher.

slides.heading: Topology sets the rules for communication resilience; devices make the forwarding happen
slides.bodyText: Choose a topology that matches your budget, reliability needs, and expected traffic patterns.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: OSI & TCP/IP Models

slides.heading: A message crossing the internet is handled by invisible layers — each with one job
slides.bodyText: Layering makes networking manageable; each layer solves a specific problem and trusts the others.

slides.heading: The OSI model has 7 layers; TCP/IP has 4 layers that actually run the internet
slides.bodyText: OSI: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. TCP/IP: Network Interface, Internet, Transport, Application. Each adds its own header (encapsulation) and passes data down.

slides.heading: Data is wrapped on the way out and unwrapped on the way in
slides.bodyText: At the sending side, each layer adds a header (or trailer). The receiving side peels them off in reverse, like opening nested boxes. This is called encapsulation and decapsulation.

slides.heading: OSI is a teaching tool; TCP/IP is what the internet actually uses
slides.bodyText: The 7‑layer OSI model is great for conceptual understanding. The 4‑layer TCP/IP model is leaner and matches real implementation. They share similar layers (Network ↔ Internet, Transport, Application).

slides.heading: Layering isolates complexity — each layer minds its own business and trusts the neighbours
slides.bodyText: This modularity allows us to change one layer (e.g., physical media) without rewriting the whole stack.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Physical Layer

slides.heading: Bits don't travel by magic — they need a medium and a way to represent 0s and 1s
slides.bodyText: The physical layer turns digital data into electrical, optical, or radio signals.

slides.heading: The physical layer defines transmission media, modes, and protocols
slides.bodyText: Media: twisted pair, fibre optic, coaxial, wireless. Modes: simplex (one way), half‑duplex (both ways but not simultaneously), full‑duplex (both ways at once). Protocols handle bit timing and encoding.

slides.heading: Bits are converted to signals, sent over a medium, and received
slides.bodyText: A transmitter encodes bits into voltage levels or light pulses. The signal travels through the medium, experiences attenuation and noise, and the receiver decodes it back into bits.

slides.heading: Wired media are reliable and fast; wireless offers mobility but more interference
slides.bodyText: Fibre optics give huge bandwidth and long distance but are costly. Wireless (Wi‑Fi, cellular) is convenient but susceptible to signal degradation and eavesdropping.

slides.heading: The physical layer is the foundation — if signals don't get through, nothing higher works
slides.bodyText: It's all about moving raw bits reliably from point A to point B.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Data Link Layer

slides.heading: Bits become frames, and frames need a way to know where one ends and the next begins
slides.bodyText: That's framing — the data link layer's first job.

slides.heading: The data link layer packages bits into frames and handles error/flow control
slides.bodyText: It adds source and destination MAC addresses, performs error detection (CRC), and manages flow control to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. It also supports switching and VLANs.

slides.heading: A frame is created, transmitted, and verified
slides.bodyText: The sender assembles a frame with header, payload, and trailer. It transmits the frame over the physical layer. The receiver checks the frame's integrity, acknowledges if needed, and passes it to the network layer.

slides.heading: Error control (retransmission) vs flow control (pacing)
slides.bodyText: Error control (like ARQ) resends lost/corrupted frames. Flow control (like sliding window) ensures the sender doesn't outrun the receiver's buffer. They address different problems.

slides.heading: The data link layer turns an unreliable physical channel into a reliable link for the network layer
slides.bodyText: It transforms raw bits into structured frames with error checks and flow regulation.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Network Layer

slides.heading: How does data find its way across the internet? One address at a time — IP addresses
slides.bodyText: The network layer is responsible for logical addressing and routing.

slides.heading: The network layer handles IP addressing, subnetting, and routing
slides.bodyText: IPv4 (32‑bit) and IPv6 (128‑bit) identify devices globally. Classful and classless addressing (CIDR) define network sizes. Subnetting divides networks for efficiency. Routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, BGP) determine the best path.

slides.heading: A packet is forwarded hop by hop based on routing tables
slides.bodyText: The source creates an IP packet with source/destination addresses. Each router reads the destination, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet to the next hop until it reaches the destination network.

slides.heading: IPv4 is running out; IPv6 solves the address shortage but has slower adoption
slides.bodyText: IPv4 offers ~4.3 billion addresses, now exhausted. IPv6 provides 2^128 addresses and built‑in security (IPsec), but migration takes time and effort.

slides.heading: The network layer is the internet's postal service — addressing and routing packets across the globe
slides.bodyText: It ensures packets get from source to destination, even across multiple networks.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Transport Layer

slides.heading: Delivering packets is only half the job — ensuring they arrive in order and without corruption is the other
slides.bodyText: That's the transport layer's responsibility.

slides.heading: The transport layer provides end‑to‑end communication, with TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast)
slides.bodyText: TCP establishes a connection, segments data, numbers segments, and retransmits lost ones. UDP is connectionless and doesn't guarantee delivery — used for real‑time applications.

slides.heading: TCP's 3‑way handshake sets up a reliable connection
slides.bodyText: SYN (client) → SYN‑ACK (server) → ACK (client). After that, data flows with sequence numbers and acknowledgements. The connection is torn down with a FIN handshake.

slides.heading: TCP is reliable but slower; UDP is fast but lossy — choose based on need
slides.bodyText: TCP guarantees delivery and order, but has overhead. UDP skips acknowledgements, perfect for streaming, gaming, and VoIP where occasional loss is acceptable.

slides.heading: The transport layer bridges the network layer and the application — it ensures data gets to the right port and is correct
slides.bodyText: It provides multiplexing, error control, and flow control between hosts.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Session Layer

slides.heading: How do two applications keep a conversation going over time? They establish a session
slides.bodyText: The session layer manages dialogues between end‑user applications.

slides.heading: The session layer sets up, manages, and tears down communication sessions
slides.bodyText: It provides services like authentication, authorisation, and full‑duplex or half‑duplex control. Protocols like NetBIOS, RPC, and PPTP operate here.

slides.heading: A session is created, used, then ended
slides.bodyText: The session layer establishes a connection (dialogue), synchronises data exchange (checkpoints), and gracefully terminates the session when done. Checkpoints allow resuming after failure.

slides.heading: The session layer is often combined with the presentation layer in the TCP/IP model
slides.bodyText: In OSI, they are separate. In TCP/IP, their functions are absorbed into the application layer. Many modern applications handle session management themselves.

slides.heading: The session layer keeps application conversations organised, with the ability to resume after interruptions
slides.bodyText: It adds structure to long‑lived interactions between programs.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Presentation Layer

slides.heading: Different systems use different formats for data — how do they understand each other?
slides.bodyText: The presentation layer translates, encrypts, and compresses data.

slides.heading: The presentation layer handles data representation, encryption, and compression
slides.bodyText: It ensures that data from one system (e.g., ASCII) is readable by another (e.g., Unicode). It may also encrypt data for security and compress it to save bandwidth.

slides.heading: Data is converted, secured, and compressed before delivery
slides.bodyText: The sender's application produces data; the presentation layer translates it to a standard format, optionally encrypts and compresses it; the receiver reverses these steps.

slides.heading: Encryption protects confidentiality; compression saves bandwidth — both add overhead
slides.bodyText: Encryption is essential for privacy but requires CPU time. Compression reduces data size but adds latency. The choice depends on the sensitivity of data and network constraints.

slides.heading: The presentation layer makes sure that data is in a usable, secure, and compact form for the application
slides.bodyText: It abstracts away differences in data formats between systems.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Application Layer

slides.heading: HTTP, Email, CDN — these are the protocols you actually interact with every day
slides.bodyText: The application layer is where users and applications meet the network.

slides.heading: The application layer provides services directly to end‑user applications
slides.bodyText: HTTP/HTTPS for web browsing, SMTP/POP3/IMAP for email, DNS for name resolution, CDN for content delivery. These protocols define how applications exchange data.

slides.heading: A web request goes through HTTP from browser to server
slides.bodyText: Your browser sends an HTTP GET request to the server. The server responds with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The browser renders the page. CDNs cache static assets to speed up delivery.

slides.heading: HTTP is plain bodyText; HTTPS adds TLS encryption; CDN distributes content globally
slides.bodyText: HTTP is insecure — anyone can read it. HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS, ensuring privacy and integrity. CDNs replicate content to edge servers, reducing latency for users worldwide.

slides.heading: The application layer is the one users see — it turns network packets into meaningful services
slides.bodyText: It's the top of the stack, where data becomes useful.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Miscellaneous Topics: Bluetooth, Ethernet, WiFi, Firewall

posts.title: Miscellaneous Topics: Bluetooth, Ethernet, WiFi, Firewall

slides.heading: Beyond the internet, everyday devices connect through Bluetooth, Ethernet, and WiFi — and firewalls guard them
slides.bodyText: These technologies are the building blocks of personal and local networks.

slides.heading: Ethernet is wired LAN; WiFi is wireless LAN; Bluetooth is short‑range personal area networking; Firewalls filter traffic
slides.bodyText: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) uses cables for reliable, high‑speed connections. WiFi (IEEE 802.11) uses radio waves for mobility. Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) connects peripherals over short distances. Firewalls enforce security policies by allowing/blocking packets.

slides.heading: Each technology works at different layers and for different use cases
slides.bodyText: Ethernet and WiFi operate at the data link and physical layers. Bluetooth also at physical/link. Firewalls operate at network/transport layers (and sometimes application). They all work together to connect and protect devices.

slides.heading: Ethernet is fast and stable; WiFi offers mobility; Bluetooth is low‑power and short‑range
slides.bodyText: Ethernet is best for desktops and servers. WiFi is for laptops and mobile devices. Bluetooth is for headphones, keyboards, and IoT. Firewalls are essential for any network exposed to the internet.

slides.heading: These technologies extend networking to every corner of our lives — connecting devices, enabling mobility, and keeping us secure
slides.bodyText: Understanding them completes the picture of how modern networks operate.

slides.heading: You've covered Computer Networks from the ground up
slides.bodyText: From bits to applications — and everything in between.

posts.title: HTML: The Skeleton of Every Website

slides.heading: Turn off CSS and JavaScript and a website is still there — just bare
slides.bodyText: That skeleton is HTML.

slides.heading: HTML defines the structure and meaning of a page, not its looks
slides.bodyText: Headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images — HTML says what each piece of content is, in a tree of nested elements.

slides.heading: The browser parses HTML into a tree it can display and script
slides.bodyText: Tags become nodes in the DOM; that tree is what CSS styles and JavaScript manipulates later.

slides.heading: Semantic HTML costs a little discipline and pays back in accessibility and SEO
slides.bodyText: Using the right element (nav, article, button) instead of generic divs takes thought, but screen readers and search engines rely on that meaning.

slides.heading: HTML is the skeleton — it decides what's on the page, before anything decides how it looks
slides.bodyText: Structure first; style and behaviour come after.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: CSS: Making the Web Actually Look Good

posts.title: CSS: Making the Web Actually Look Good

slides.heading: The same HTML can look like a spreadsheet or a magazine — CSS is the difference
slides.bodyText: Style lives entirely outside the structure.

slides.heading: CSS controls how HTML looks: layout, colour, spacing, type
slides.bodyText: It's a separate language of rules that select elements and describe their appearance and position.

slides.heading: Selectors target elements; the box model and layout systems position them
slides.bodyText: You point at elements with selectors, then use the box model, flexbox, or grid to control size, spacing, and arrangement.

slides.heading: Separating style from structure keeps both clean but adds specificity puzzles
slides.bodyText: Splitting looks from content means you can restyle without touching HTML; the cost is cascade and specificity rules that decide which conflicting style wins.

slides.heading: HTML says what it is; CSS says how it looks — keep the two jobs apart and both stay sane
slides.bodyText: Presentation is a separate concern from meaning.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: JavaScript Basics: Making Pages Interactive

slides.heading: HTML and CSS give you a page that just sits there — clicking anything does nothing
slides.bodyText: JavaScript is what makes it react.

slides.heading: JavaScript adds behaviour: it responds to events and changes the page live
slides.bodyText: It runs in the browser, listens for clicks and input, and updates the DOM without reloading.

slides.heading: An event fires, your code runs, the DOM changes, the user sees it
slides.bodyText: A button click triggers a function; that function reads or rewrites the page's elements; the browser re-renders the affected part.

slides.heading: More interactivity means more client-side code to load, run, and maintain
slides.bodyText: Rich behaviour improves the experience but ships more script to every visitor and adds state that can get out of sync with the page.

slides.heading: HTML and CSS build the page; JavaScript is what lets it respond to the person using it
slides.bodyText: Structure, style, then behaviour — the third layer brings it alive.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Closures, Promises & Async/Await: JS Gets Real

posts.title: Closures, Promises & Async/Await: JS Gets Real

slides.heading: Your code asks for data, then immediately uses it — and gets 'undefined'
slides.bodyText: The data hadn't arrived yet. Welcome to async.

slides.heading: Closures capture state; promises and async/await handle work that finishes later
slides.bodyText: A closure remembers the variables around it; a promise represents a value that isn't ready yet; async/await lets you write that waiting as if it were sequential.

slides.heading: Kick off slow work, keep going, and handle the result when it lands
slides.bodyText: Instead of freezing while a network request runs, JavaScript registers what to do when it completes and moves on — then resumes with the result.

slides.heading: Async keeps the UI responsive but makes control flow harder to follow
slides.bodyText: Non-blocking code means the page never freezes on a slow call; the cost is reasoning about code that doesn't run top-to-bottom in order.

slides.heading: A promise is an IOU for a value; async/await lets you wait for it without freezing everything else
slides.bodyText: Asynchrony trades linear reading for a responsive program.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Fetch, APIs & JS Modules

slides.heading: A modern web app is mostly your page asking other servers for data, constantly
slides.bodyText: fetch is how it asks.

slides.heading: fetch calls APIs; modules organise JS into reusable, isolated files
slides.bodyText: fetch sends HTTP requests from the browser and returns a promise; ES modules let you split code into files that explicitly import and export what they share.

slides.heading: Request data, await the response, parse it, update the page
slides.bodyText: Your code fetches from an API endpoint, waits for the JSON, turns it into objects, and renders them — no page reload needed.

slides.heading: Splitting into modules improves clarity but adds build and dependency complexity
slides.bodyText: Small, focused files are easier to reason about and reuse; the trade is a build step and a dependency graph to manage.

slides.heading: fetch is how the browser talks to servers; modules are how you keep the code that does it organised
slides.bodyText: The modern front end is requests and reusable pieces.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Library vs Framework: Why React Exists

posts.title: Library vs Framework: Why React Exists

slides.heading: You can build a UI with plain JavaScript — until the app grows and the manual DOM updates become unmanageable
slides.bodyText: That's the gap frameworks fill.

slides.heading: A library you call; a framework calls you — React sits in between and owns the rendering
slides.bodyText: With a library, your code is in charge; a framework provides the structure and runs your code within it. React manages when and how the UI updates.

slides.heading: You describe the UI for a given state; React updates the DOM to match
slides.bodyText: Instead of manually changing elements, you write what the page should look like for the current data, and React figures out the minimal DOM changes.

slides.heading: A framework saves boilerplate but imposes its conventions and learning curve
slides.bodyText: You write far less repetitive UI code and gain structure; you also buy into its way of doing things and its update cycle.

slides.heading: A library is a tool you pick up; a framework is a house you move into — React trades freedom for structure
slides.bodyText: You give up manual control to stop managing the DOM by hand.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: State, Routing & Server-Side Rendering

slides.heading: Your app remembers what the user did, shows the right page, and loads fast on first paint
slides.bodyText: State, routing, and rendering strategy are doing that.

slides.heading: State is the app's live data; routing maps URLs to views; SSR renders on the server first
slides.bodyText: State drives what's shown; routing decides which component a URL displays; server-side rendering sends ready-made HTML before the JS loads.

slides.heading: Server renders the first view, the browser takes over, state drives everything after
slides.bodyText: SSR delivers a fast, visible page; then client-side code hydrates it and manages state and navigation without full reloads.

slides.heading: SSR improves first load and SEO but costs server work; client rendering is lighter on the server but slower to first paint
slides.bodyText: Rendering on the server gets content visible sooner and crawlable; doing it in the browser offloads the server but shows a blank page longer.

slides.heading: State is what changes, routing is where you are, SSR is who draws the first frame — the three levers of a modern app
slides.bodyText: Where and when you render is an architecture decision, not a detail.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Node.js & Express: JavaScript on the Backend

posts.title: Node.js & Express: JavaScript on the Backend

slides.heading: JavaScript was trapped in the browser for years — then Node let it run the server too
slides.bodyText: Now one language spans both ends.

slides.heading: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser; Express structures the server code
slides.bodyText: Node gives JS access to files, networks, and the OS; Express is a minimal framework for defining routes and handling HTTP requests on top of it.

slides.heading: A request hits a route, your handler runs, a response goes back
slides.bodyText: Express matches the URL and method to a handler function; that function does the work — query a database, shape data — and returns a response.

slides.heading: One language across the stack speeds teams up but Node's single thread punishes heavy CPU work
slides.bodyText: Sharing JS front-to-back reduces conbodyText switching; Node's event loop shines at many I/O tasks and stalls on one heavy computation.

slides.heading: Node put JavaScript on the server; Express gave it a clean way to answer requests
slides.bodyText: The browser language became a full-stack language.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: REST APIs, Auth & Authorization Explained

slides.heading: Your app needs to let the right people do the right things — and block everyone else
slides.bodyText: That's auth, and it's two separate questions.

slides.heading: A REST API exposes resources over HTTP; authentication is who you are, authorization is what you may do
slides.bodyText: REST maps URLs to resources and verbs to actions; authentication proves identity; authorization checks permissions.

slides.heading: Verify the user, then check whether that user is allowed this action
slides.bodyText: First confirm identity (login, token); then, on each request, decide if this identity has the right to the resource — two checks, in order.

slides.heading: Confusing authentication with authorization is a classic, dangerous bug
slides.bodyText: Proving someone is logged in isn't the same as proving they may delete this record; skip the second check and any user can act as any other.

slides.heading: Authentication asks 'who are you?'; authorization asks 'are you allowed?' — never merge the two
slides.bodyText: Identity and permission are different gates.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Cookies, Sessions, JWT, Middleware & WebSockets

slides.heading: HTTP forgets you the instant a request ends — so how does a site keep you logged in?
slides.bodyText: With one of several ways to carry state.

slides.heading: Cookies, sessions, and JWTs carry identity across stateless requests; middleware and WebSockets extend the server
slides.bodyText: A cookie stores a token in the browser; a session keeps state on the server; a JWT is a signed, self-contained token. Middleware processes requests in a pipeline; WebSockets keep a connection open for real-time data.

slides.heading: Log in once, get a token, send it with every later request
slides.bodyText: The server issues a session ID or JWT; the browser returns it on each request so the server recognises you without asking again.

slides.heading: Server sessions are easy to revoke but hold state; JWTs scale statelessly but are hard to invalidate early
slides.bodyText: Sessions can be killed instantly but need shared storage; JWTs need no lookup and scale well, but a leaked token stays valid until it expires.

slides.heading: HTTP is forgetful; cookies, sessions, and tokens are how a site remembers you between requests
slides.bodyText: Statelessness is the default — identity is something you carry back each time.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Why Do We Even Need Databases?

slides.heading: A spreadsheet is fine until your customer's name appears three ways — and you lose trust
slides.bodyText: Databases exist to keep data consistent, safe, and queryable — even under heavy use.

slides.heading: A database is a structured, persistent, and logically cohesive collection of related data
slides.bodyText: A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that manages that data, enforcing integrity, security, and concurrent access. It abstracts physical storage and provides logical views.

slides.heading: Data is defined, stored, manipulated, and retrieved through a DBMS
slides.bodyText: You define a schema (structure), insert data, run queries (SQL), and the DBMS handles indexing, caching, and transaction management behind the scenes.

slides.heading: File systems are simple but chaotic; DBMS adds order, safety, and power
slides.bodyText: Files cause redundancy, inconsistency, and lack of concurrent access. DBMS provides centralised control, ACID transactions, and declarative querying — at the cost of complexity.

slides.heading: A DBMS is a file system that knows how to be shared, queried, and kept correct under pressure
slides.bodyText: It turns raw storage into a trusted source of truth.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Entity Relationship Model

slides.heading: Before you write a single table, you need to understand the world you're modelling
