slides.heading: CNNs scan for local patterns; RNNs carry memory; transformers weigh every token against every other
slides.bodyText: A CNN slides filters over an image to detect features; an RNN passes a hidden state along a sequence; a transformer lets each element attend directly to all others in parallel.

slides.heading: Transformers parallelise and capture long-range conbodyText but are compute- and data-hungry
slides.bodyText: RNNs process sequentially and forget distant conbodyText; transformers see everything at once and scale better, at the cost of far more computation and data.

slides.heading: CNNs see space, RNNs remember sequence, transformers attend to everything at once — architecture follows the data's shape
slides.bodyText: The transformer won by relating every token to every other in parallel.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: What Is Generative AI & What Is an LLM?

posts.title: What Is Generative AI & What Is an LLM?

slides.heading: Predictive AI labels what exists; generative AI produces what didn't — that's a genuine shift
slides.bodyText: And an LLM is the engine behind the bodyText kind.

slides.heading: Generative AI creates new content; an LLM is a model trained to predict the next token
slides.bodyText: Instead of classifying inputs, generative models produce new bodyText, images, or audio; a large language model does this for bodyText by repeatedly predicting the most likely next piece.

slides.heading: Predict the next token, append it, repeat — coherent bodyText emerges
slides.bodyText: Given the bodyText so far, the model outputs a probability over possible next tokens, picks one, adds it, and repeats — fluent output from a loop of predictions.

slides.heading: LLMs generate fluent, flexible bodyText but can state falsehoods confidently
slides.bodyText: Next-token prediction produces remarkably capable, general bodyText; the same mechanism has no built-in grasp of truth, so it can be fluently, confidently wrong.

slides.heading: An LLM doesn't retrieve answers — it predicts the next token, one at a time, until it has a response
slides.bodyText: Fluency is prediction, not knowledge — which is why it can be sure and wrong.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Tokens & ConbodyText Windows: How LLMs Actually Read bodyText

posts.title: Tokens & ConbodyText Windows: How LLMs Actually Read bodyText

slides.heading: An LLM never sees your words — it sees numbered chunks, and it can only hold so many at once
slides.bodyText: Those chunks are tokens, and the ceiling on how many fit is the conbodyText window.

slides.heading: A token is a piece of bodyText; the conbodyText window is how many fit at once
slides.bodyText: bodyText is split into tokens — roughly word-pieces — each mapped to a number; the model can only attend to a fixed number of them per request.

slides.heading: Your prompt, the retrieved docs, and the reply all compete for one window
slides.bodyText: Prompt, conversation history, retrieved conbodyText, and the answer share a single token budget; overflow it and the earliest content falls out of view.

slides.heading: A bigger conbodyText window sees more but costs more and can lose focus
slides.bodyText: More tokens let the model consider more at once; they also cost more per call and can dilute attention across a huge window — bigger isn't free, or always better.

slides.heading: An LLM reads in tokens and thinks inside a fixed window — everything you send competes for that space
slides.bodyText: The conbodyText window is the model's entire field of view.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers Demystified

slides.heading: How does a model that only does math understand that 'king' and 'queen' are related?
slides.bodyText: Embeddings and attention are the answer.

slides.heading: Embeddings turn words into vectors of meaning; attention lets tokens weigh each other; transformers combine both
slides.bodyText: An embedding places each token in a space where similar meanings sit close; attention lets each token decide which others matter for it; the transformer stacks this into understanding.

slides.heading: Embed tokens into vectors, then let attention mix in the relevant conbodyText
slides.bodyText: Words become numeric vectors capturing meaning; attention updates each token's representation using the tokens it deems relevant, so 'bank' near 'river' differs from 'bank' near 'money'.

slides.heading: Attention captures conbodyText brilliantly but its cost grows with the square of sequence length
slides.bodyText: Relating every token to every other gives rich conbodyText understanding; that all-pairs comparison makes long inputs expensive — the core scaling challenge of transformers.

slides.heading: Embeddings give tokens meaning, attention gives them conbodyText — together they let math 'understand' language
slides.bodyText: Meaning is a position in space; conbodyText is what attention pulls in.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Temperature & Sampling: Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers

posts.title: Temperature & Sampling: Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers

slides.heading: You sent the identical prompt twice and got two different answers — that's not a bug
slides.bodyText: It's the sampling settings deciding how much randomness to allow.

slides.heading: The model outputs probabilities; sampling picks which token to actually use
slides.bodyText: At each step it ranks every possible next token; temperature and top-p control how far it's willing to stray from the single most likely one.

slides.heading: Low temperature is focused and repeatable; high temperature is varied and creative
slides.bodyText: Near zero it almost always picks the top token — consistent, sometimes bland; higher, it samples further down the list — more variety, more risk of nonsense.

slides.heading: Deterministic output is reliable but rigid; sampled output is creative but inconsistent
slides.bodyText: Set it low for facts, code, and anything you need repeatable; set it higher for brainstorming and copy — the right setting depends on whether you want the same answer twice.

slides.heading: Temperature is the model's boldness dial — low for correct, high for creative
slides.bodyText: Same prompt, different answers is a setting, not a fault.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Prompting, System Prompts & Structured Outputs

slides.heading: The same model gives a mediocre or an excellent answer depending only on how you asked
slides.bodyText: Prompting is a real skill, not a trick.

slides.heading: The prompt is your instruction; the system prompt sets behaviour; structured outputs force a usable format
slides.bodyText: What you type steers the model; a system prompt shapes its role and rules across the whole session; asking for JSON or a schema makes output a program can parse.

slides.heading: Set the role, give clear instructions and examples, and specify the output shape
slides.bodyText: You establish conbodyText and constraints in a system prompt, state the task precisely with examples, and request a defined format so the response is predictable and machine-readable.

slides.heading: Clear, constrained prompts improve reliability but can reduce creative range
slides.bodyText: Tight instructions and formats make outputs consistent and parseable; over-constraining can box the model out of better, more flexible answers — match the leash to the task.

slides.heading: The model's quality is bounded by your prompt — vague in, vague out; precise in, usable out
slides.bodyText: How you ask is part of the system, not a footnote.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Why LLMs Hallucinate (And What Actually Reduces It)

posts.title: Why LLMs Hallucinate (And What Actually Reduces It)

slides.heading: An LLM cited a court case that never existed — confidently, in perfect legal formatting
slides.bodyText: It wasn't lying; it was doing exactly what it's built to do.

slides.heading: A hallucination is fluent bodyText that isn't true — a side effect of next-token prediction
slides.bodyText: The model optimizes for plausible continuations, not verified facts; when it doesn't know, it still produces the most likely-sounding answer.

slides.heading: Grounding the model in real sources is what reduces it
slides.bodyText: Retrieval feeds it actual documents to answer from, and asking for citations or 'I don't know' lowers confident invention — you constrain it toward evidence.

slides.heading: Fluency and factuality are different targets, and the base model optimizes for the first
slides.bodyText: The same mechanism that makes output sound expert makes it sound expert when it's wrong — cutting hallucination means adding truth constraints the model doesn't have on its own.

slides.heading: An LLM predicts what sounds right, not what is right — grounding it in sources is how you close the gap
slides.bodyText: Confidence is not evidence; fluency is not fact.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Fine-Tuning, RAG & Vector Databases

slides.heading: An LLM knows nothing about your private documents and can't learn today's news on its own
slides.bodyText: Fine-tuning and RAG solve two different halves of that.

slides.heading: Fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights; RAG retrieves facts at query time from a vector database
slides.bodyText: Fine-tuning teaches new behaviour or style by training on examples; RAG leaves the model unchanged and instead fetches relevant documents to include in the prompt.

slides.heading: Embed your documents, retrieve the relevant ones, and feed them to the model with the question
slides.bodyText: Your data is turned into vectors and stored; at query time the most relevant chunks are retrieved and added to the prompt so the model answers from real, current sources.

slides.heading: Fine-tuning changes behaviour but is costly and static; RAG adds fresh knowledge but depends on retrieval quality
slides.bodyText: Fine-tuning bakes in style and skills yet must be redone as data changes; RAG updates instantly by swapping documents but only helps if it retrieves the right ones.

slides.heading: Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves; RAG changes what it knows right now — different problems, different tools
slides.bodyText: Teach behaviour by tuning; supply knowledge by retrieving.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Why Chatbots Aren't Agents (And What Actually Makes an Agent)

posts.title: Why Chatbots Aren't Agents (And What Actually Makes an Agent)

slides.heading: A chatbot answers and stops; you asked it to 'book the trip' and it just... described how to
slides.bodyText: The gap between those is what makes an agent.

slides.heading: An agent doesn't just respond — it takes actions in a loop to achieve a goal
slides.bodyText: A chatbot maps input to output once; an agent plans, uses tools, observes results, and keeps going until the goal is met or it gives up.

slides.heading: Reason about the goal, act with a tool, observe, then decide the next step
slides.bodyText: Given an objective, the agent chooses an action, executes it (search, API call, code), reads the outcome, and loops — using each result to inform the next move.

slides.heading: Agents accomplish multi-step goals but add unpredictability and failure modes chatbots don't have
slides.bodyText: Autonomy lets them actually do things across steps; it also means they can loop, take wrong actions, or compound errors — capability and risk rise together.

slides.heading: A chatbot responds; an agent acts, observes, and decides again — the loop is what makes it an agent
slides.bodyText: The difference isn't smarter answers, it's taking steps toward a goal.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Tool Calling, Memory & Planning: How Agents Think

posts.title: Tool Calling, Memory & Planning: How Agents Think

slides.heading: A model alone can't check the weather, remember yesterday, or break a big task into steps
slides.bodyText: Tools, memory, and planning are the scaffolding that give it those abilities.

slides.heading: Tool calling lets an agent act, memory lets it retain conbodyText, planning lets it sequence steps
slides.bodyText: Tools connect the model to the real world (search, APIs, code); memory persists information across turns and sessions; planning decomposes a goal into ordered sub-tasks.

slides.heading: Plan the steps, call tools to execute them, store results in memory for later steps
slides.bodyText: The agent breaks a goal into sub-tasks, invokes the right tool for each, and writes outcomes to memory so later steps can build on earlier ones.

slides.heading: More tools and memory expand capability but widen the attack and error surface
slides.bodyText: Each tool an agent can call and each thing it remembers makes it more capable and gives more ways to be misused, poisoned, or to go wrong — power and risk scale together.

slides.heading: Tools let an agent act, memory lets it remember, planning lets it sequence — capability comes from the model plus its scaffolding
slides.bodyText: The intelligence is the model; the usefulness is the scaffolding around it.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Agent Loops, Multi-Step Tasks & Real-World Agents

posts.title: Agent Loops, Multi-Step Tasks & Real-World Agents

slides.heading: Real tasks aren't one step — 'research this and write a summary' is a dozen actions in sequence
slides.bodyText: The agent loop is what strings them together.

slides.heading: The agent loop repeats reason-act-observe until a multi-step task is done
slides.bodyText: Each cycle the agent decides the next action, executes it, and evaluates the result, continuing until the goal is reached or a stopping condition triggers.

slides.heading: Loop: decide, act, observe, check if done — repeat or stop
slides.bodyText: The agent assesses progress, takes the next action, reads the outcome, and either continues the loop or ends — with limits to prevent it running forever.

slides.heading: Longer loops handle harder tasks but risk drift, cost, and runaway execution
slides.bodyText: More iterations let agents tackle complex goals; they also accumulate cost, can wander off-task, and need guardrails and step limits so a stuck agent doesn't loop endlessly.

slides.heading: An agent handles multi-step work by looping reason-act-observe until it's done — with a leash so it stops
slides.bodyText: Real-world tasks are loops, not single replies.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: AI Workflows, Multi-Agent Systems & MCP

slides.heading: One agent doing everything gets confused; a fixed script can't adapt — the middle ground is structure
slides.bodyText: Workflows, multi-agent systems, and MCP provide it.

slides.heading: Workflows are predefined paths; multi-agent systems split work across specialised agents; MCP standardises tool access
slides.bodyText: A workflow fixes the steps for reliability; multiple agents each own a role and coordinate; the Model ConbodyText Protocol gives models a standard way to connect to tools and data.

slides.heading: Use fixed workflows where reliability matters, agents where flexibility does, MCP to connect both to tools
slides.bodyText: Predictable tasks run as workflows; open-ended ones use agents; MCP provides a common interface so any of them can reach external systems the same way.

slides.heading: Workflows are predictable but rigid; multi-agent systems are flexible but harder to control
slides.bodyText: Fixed paths give reliability and are easy to reason about; autonomous agents adapt to the unexpected but coordinate unpredictably — most real systems blend the two.

slides.heading: Workflows give reliability, agents give flexibility, MCP gives them a common way to reach the world
slides.bodyText: Choose structure where you need certainty and autonomy where you need adaptability.

slides.heading: Coming next
slides.bodyText: Evaluating & Securing Production AI Agents

slides.heading: An agent that can act can also act wrongly — or be tricked into it — at machine speed
slides.bodyText: Evaluation and security aren't optional for production agents.

slides.heading: Evaluation measures whether the agent actually works; security defends against misuse like prompt injection
slides.bodyText: Evals test task success, cost, and failure rates systematically; security guards against manipulated inputs, tool misuse, and leaking data the agent shouldn't touch.

slides.heading: Test on real tasks, constrain tool permissions, and watch for injected instructions
slides.bodyText: You benchmark the agent on representative tasks, limit each tool to least privilege, and validate inputs so hidden instructions in fetched content can't hijack it.

slides.heading: Broad autonomy is powerful but every capability is also a new attack vector
slides.bodyText: The more an agent can do, the more useful and the more dangerous when compromised; locking it down reduces risk and also the very autonomy that made it valuable.

slides.heading: A production agent must be measured and constrained — capability without evaluation and guardrails is a liability
slides.bodyText: Powerful and unchecked is not deployable; test it and fence it.

slides.bodyText: Building Your First AI Agent (Then a Multi-Agent System)

posts.title: Building Your First AI Agent (Then a Multi-Agent System)

slides.heading: The gap from 'I understand agents' to 'I built one' is smaller than it looks — and one agent leads to many
slides.bodyText: Here's the shape of building it.

slides.heading: A first agent is a model, a set of tools, and a loop; a multi-agent system coordinates several
slides.bodyText: Give a model access to tools and wrap it in a reason-act-observe loop and you have an agent; give each of several agents a role and a way to hand off, and you have a system.

slides.heading: Start with one agent and a few tools, then split roles as the task grows
slides.bodyText: Build a single agent that plans and calls tools; when the task spans distinct skills, break it into specialised agents that pass work between them.

slides.heading: Multi-agent systems handle bigger problems but add coordination and failure complexity
slides.bodyText: Splitting work across agents scales to harder tasks and cleaner responsibilities; it also introduces communication overhead and new ways for the system to deadlock or misfire.

slides.heading: An agent is a model, tools, and a loop; a multi-agent system is several of those learning to hand off
slides.bodyText: Start with one agent that works, then divide the labour.

posts.title: The Entire Journey: From Computer to AI Agent

slides.heading: You started at 'why do computers exist' and arrived at building AI agents — that's not 121 tips, it's one system
slides.bodyText: Here's how every piece connected.

slides.heading: The whole journey is layers of abstraction, each built on the one below
slides.bodyText: Hardware runs machine code, the OS manages it, languages express logic, networks connect machines, the web and databases build on them, and AI sits at the very top of that stack.

slides.heading: Each track answered 'what does the layer below make possible?'
slides.bodyText: Transistors enabled processors, processors ran operating systems, those ran programs, programs formed networks and the web, and all of it became the substrate for data systems and AI.

slides.heading: Understanding the whole stack beats memorising any single layer
slides.bodyText: Knowing one technology deeply is useful; seeing how every layer enables the next is what lets you reason about systems you've never seen before — that's the real payoff.

slides.heading: You don't just know more technologies — you understand how the pieces fit into one system
slides.bodyText: From a switch to an agent, it was always one stack, one journey.

slides.heading: You finished the journey
slides.bodyText: One system, end to end — from a single switch to autonomous AI agents.
